# Copyright for authors (`copyright`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by printing_press, woodblock_printing, patents
- Core idea: The author of a book, map, engraving or piece of music has the sole right to print and sell it for a limited term, after which anyone may reprint it. Before printing, copying was slow and nobody needed the rule; after it, a printer who pays an author is undercut at once by one who does not, so careful new works go unpaid. A workable law vests the right in the author (who may sell it to a printer), sets a term of some 14 to 28 years, requires registration and deposit of a copy, and leaves ideas and facts free.
- Pitfalls:
  - Granting a perpetual right to a printers' guild: this is a censorship tool and a monopoly on old books, as with the London Stationers' Company
  - Trying to protect ideas, facts or methods rather than the particular text or image
  - Forgetting that it stops at the border: Dutch, Irish and American printers freely reprinted foreign works until the Berne Convention (1886)
- History: china: c. 1190s – Song printed books carry notices that the work is registered with the authorities and reprinting is forbidden; protection by case-by-case petition, no general law; europe: 1469 – Venice gives John of Speyer a five-year monopoly on printing; 1486 first known privilege to an author (Sabellico, Venice); 1557 Stationers' Company charter; 1710 Statute of Anne: 14 years, renewable once, vested in authors; 1886 Berne Convention; americas: 1790 – US Copyright Act, 14 years renewable once
- Read:
  - Adrian Johns, Piracy: The Intellectual Property Wars from Gutenberg to Gates (2009)
  - Mark Rose, Authors and Owners: The Invention of Copyright (1993)
